title: Research
text:
PD-1–PD-L1 signaling in neonatal heart regeneration (2024, Nature Cardiovascular Research 3(3), 389–402)
In this work, I show that the PD-1–PD-L1 immune checkpoint pathway is highly active in the neonatal heart and is required for successful regeneration after myocardial infarction. Disruption of this pathway alters γδ T cell behavior, promoting autoreactive features, excessive inflammation, and fibrotic repair. These findings establish that neonatal heart regeneration does not simply occur in the setting of an immature immune system, but instead depends on active immune regulation that keeps the injury response compatible with regeneration.
A γδT17–IL-17A axis supports neonatal heart regeneration (2026, Cell Reports 45(10), 118100)
In this work, I characterize a population of γδT17 cells that accumulates in the injured heart specifically during the regenerative window and promotes regeneration through IL-17A. Mechanistically, γδT17-derived IL-17A acts primarily on myeloid cells to initiate a rapid, self-limited inflammatory response that supports injury resolution. This study links immune development to regenerative competence by showing that the neonatal heart can transiently engage a specialized immune population that is largely absent from the later injury response. It also shows that inflammatory signaling is not inherently detrimental to regeneration: when appropriately timed and rapidly resolved, it can actively support tissue repair.

T cell-mediated regulation of mouse neonatal heart regeneration. American Heart Association, October 2025 – October 2028 (Award No. 25CDA1454364). This project studies how neonatal γδ T cells and IL-17A support heart regeneration and whether IL-17A can improve repair after the regenerative window closes.

Stephanie Vargas Aguilar
Postdoctoral fellow · Olson Lab
UT Southwestern Medical Center
How does the immune system heal the heart?
Lessons from newborns

title: About
text:
Why do several mammalian tissues regenerate early in life yet lose this capacity soon after birth?
Most explanations for the closure of this regenerative window have focused on maturation of the injured tissue itself: changes in proliferative capacity, metabolism, or extracellular matrix. Yet the immune system is undergoing an equally dramatic transformation during this same period, and its contribution to regenerative decline remains underappreciated.
I am an Ecuadorian immunologist interested in how changes in the immune system across the lifespan shape tissue function, repair, and regeneration. I currently conduct research in the laboratory of Dr. Eric Olson at UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas, where I study the immune mechanisms that enable the mammalian neonatal heart to regenerate after injury. A major goal of my work is to determine whether immune mechanisms that support neonatal regeneration can be harnessed to improve adult tissue repair.
My research combines mouse genetics, immune profiling, lineage tracing, and single cell genomic approaches, and is currently supported by a Career Development Award from the American Heart Association.
Beyond the laboratory, I am interested in building stronger connections between scientists in the Global South and Global North, giving greater visibility to Latin American research, and encouraging young people to consider science as a possible career.
